doc.title: Roscoe Mitchell interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 23, 2023

title: Art from his mother's side, music from his father's side
summary: Uncles Charles Commodore Carter and Arthur were artists; his father, a singer who lost his voice, urged him to sing and then backed his clarinet and saxophone.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I’ll have to remember that. I like that. I’m going to take you way back for a moment if I could. Can you recall, when I look at your career and how much exploring you did, I wonder as a child, even before you started on a woodwind, were you constantly exploring sounds?

Well in a way I was. I mean I would say that like the art is on my mother’s side of the family. My uncle Charles Commodore Carter was an artist, and he had put together — what he worked with was crayon and he would layer the crayon and then he had a metal © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

protractor that he’d scrape and to blend the colors. And he did a book about my sisters and myself and our friends, and we were these people from outer space and so on. So the problem with that whole thing was you know he had moved out of our house and into the church, where he was also another pastor in there, and you know when he passed away those books are gone. And I’ve done everything you know, to try to find them and I can’t find them. But I mean they were glorious. But so the art comes from that side of the family. My uncle Arthur was also an artist and he made a lot of art toys when we were growing up. Okay? So, and then the music comes from my father’s side of the family. My father was a singer you know, at one time, and he had problems with his vocal cords so he had to stop singing, but I mean I recall him being able to, you know and back then people would be able to imitate instruments and so on, with their voice. So he was really good at that and he would always say to me, “Well you know you need to sing” you know. So I sung when I was young and he said, “Well you need to sing because saxophone players are a dime a dozen you know. But you know I mean and I did sing, like for the family and I think I was pretty good at imitating like Nat King Cole and different people. But you know when I decided to take on the clarinet and saxophone, you know he got behind whatever I wanted to do. He just wanted to see me being interested in something.
